name: Routines, the skin barrier and glass skin
short: Morning and night routines, skin cycling, the damaged barrier, glass skin and glow.
says: The comments here are detailed and practical. Under the minimalist derm routine, viewers are startled by a retinoid with no moisturizer, question skipping daily sunscreen on a retinoid, ask for a budget retinoid and cheer "less is more". Under the barrier-signs video they ask how to tell purging from a bad product, how long healing takes, and share their own perioral dermatitis cases. Run 1's questions repeat it: how long does a barrier take to heal, should I still wear sunscreen when my barrier is damaged, why does my face feel tight however much I moisturize, and routines for teens and for your 30s.

blocks.s: The biggest theme in the niche is a tug of war between more and less. On one side: glass-skin routines, K-beauty steps, PDRN creams, skin cycling and 25-product mornings, much of it sponsored. On the other: dermatologists showing a real routine of wash, retinoid, done, and reacting with horror as a creator's face reddens under 20 products. The damaged barrier is the price of overdoing it, and the fixes are boring: stop actives, moisturize damp skin, petroleum jelly or zinc cream overnight. People watch for the glow, out of fear they've wrecked their skin, and to see a doctor roast a ridiculous routine.
The numbers
107 videos, 12% of the niche. 18% of them are winners and the median one does 1.29× its creator's usual (1.08× for the ones he could make); 53% (57 videos) are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
Skin cycling (an exfoliant night, a retinoid night, then two recovery nights) gives skin that looks like an Instagram filter.
Skin cycling underdoses the exfoliant: once a week is barely more than splashing water on your face, and the whole idea is common sense packaged as marketing.
A dermatologist's real routine is wash and retinoid at night, wash in the morning, and you don't need to buy into the industry.
Nine times out of ten people moisturize wrong: put it on right after washing, while the skin is still damp.
Twenty products at once will inflame your barrier; stick to three or four hydrating basics and fix one problem at a time.
When the barrier is damaged, stop every active, retinoids included, until it heals.
Zinc oxide diaper cream on the face overnight heals a damaged barrier fast; so does a pea-size amount of Vaseline patted on.
You can get smoother skin with no acids or retinoids at all, just plain moisturizer or petroleum jelly.
K-pop idols' glass skin comes from daily barrier care with PDRN cream.
Celebrities who say "water and sleep" are hiding the clinic treatments behind their glow.
A simple cleanse, sunscreen and retinoid routine in your twenties pays off for decades.
How it sounds

It's split almost evenly between doctors (50%) and influencers (43%), and the tone is casual (40% casual-friend, 17% humor). Influencers sell steps and products (21% salesy, 14% sponsored). The doctors who win do the opposite: they open with "I'm a dermatologist" and then take things away, or they use the "Hi, dermatologist here" reaction format to mock a maximalist routine. The winning first line sets up a contradiction between what TikTok shows and what a doctor actually does.
Three opening lines that worked:
“I'm a dermatologist, and here's my real nightly routine.” (@drgazy, 52× usual)
“Nine times out of 10, I find that people are moisturizing wrong.” (@dr.mamina, 92× usual)
“Okay, so this is way too many products.” (@dermdocmalik, 29× usual)

**Maps to:** Pure Creamy Cleanser (for rosacea and post-procedure skin), Hyla Complex (barrier moisturizer), Nia-C+ (niacinamide and ceramides), the Hyaluronic Peptide Serum, the Rosacea/Redness and Anti-aging Regimen Sets, the Sun Shade sunscreens and the free skincare evaluation; in the office, DiamondGlow, HydraFacial, microinfusion and SKINVIVE (the honest "glass skin" injectable, "a healthy, dewy-looking aspect").

name: Faces: filler, fat and Ozempic face
short: Filler, buccal fat, Sculptra, under-eye hollows and the faces that weight-loss drugs leave behind.
says: Comments here are scarce: the one clip with recorded reactions is a looksmaxxing jawline joke, where viewers reply "it's genetics" and "it's over" and one warns that thumb-pulling is dangerous. The sharpest viewer voice is a run 1 comment, "are we fucking normalizing taking ozempic for non-essential purposes?", with 1,657 likes. So the audience is judging GLP-1 use as much as asking about fixes, and the claims show what worries them: looking older after weight loss, looking overfilled, and regretting something permanent.

blocks.s: This theme is about volume: who has too much, who lost it, and what fixing it does to you. The loudest strand is Ozempic face, with celebrity before-and-afters and doctors arguing whether it is the drug or just fast weight loss. Next is buccal fat removal, where derms warn that facial fat is what keeps you young and surgeons say a careful trim won't cause regret. Then the filler backlash: migration, the "filler mustache", an MRI of filler that spread. Sculptra and SkinVive are pitched as the subtler answer, while looksmaxxers try bone smashing and jaw balls. People watch because they are afraid of looking older, or looking done.
The numbers
93 videos, 10% of the niche. 14% of them are winners and the median one does 1.07× its creator's usual; 66% (61 videos) are ones Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
Ozempic face isn't caused by semaglutide itself; it is what happens to anyone who loses a lot of weight very fast.
GLP-1 weight loss thins the fat pads around the eyes and upper cheeks, unmasking hollows and tear troughs that were always there.
People with fat in their face age the best, so removing buccal fat young takes away what aging will strip for free (a cosmetic derm, 4.9× usual).
Buccal fat doesn't shrink with age like other fat, so judicious removal won't cause regret and can help in middle age too.
An MRI of a 33-year-old who had 12 cc of filler over six years measured close to 28 cc, spread across the face.
Lip filler migration causes a "filler mustache"; stop adding filler, wait out the swelling, then dissolve it.
Cross-linked filler does not simply dissolve with hyaluronidase; it migrates, persists and can be encapsulated.
Sculptra is not a filler: it triggers your own collagen over weeks to months and lasts two to three years.
SkinVive is not a filler either: tiny droplets of hyaluronic acid hydrate the skin without changing your features.
Face exercises, jaw balls and bone smashing can't add volume or reshape bone; the muscles and bones don't work that way.
How it sounds

Doctors carry the most (41%), then influencers (24%) and brands (14%). The tone splits between sales and clinic copy on one side and a clinical, contrarian, slightly alarmed voice on the other. The biggest numbers belong to silent celebrity slideshows of Ozempic faces (1594× and 314× usual), which he could only use as narrated commentary. Among makeable winners, the first line either points at a face and names the problem, or states a rule about aging that sounds like a verdict.
Three opening lines that worked:
“what you see here is called the osempic face.” (@stoffwechsel_doc, 15×)
“People that have fat in their face age the best.” (@shereeneidriss, 4.9×)
“So many girls have this special type of mustache and nobody's talking about it.” (@doctorjarrett, 4.4×)
What the audience says back

Comments here are scarce: the one clip with recorded reactions is a looksmaxxing jawline joke, where viewers reply "it's genetics" and "it's over" and one warns that thumb-pulling is dangerous. The sharpest viewer voice is a run 1 comment, "are we fucking normalizing taking ozempic for non-essential purposes?", with 1,657 likes. So the audience is judging GLP-1 use as much as asking about fixes, and the claims show what worries them: looking older after weight loss, looking overfilled, and regretting something permanent.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** HA fillers (Juvéderm and Evolysse, Restylane, Radiesse, Belotero), Sculptra, SKINVIVE, PRFM, fat transfer, the non-surgical nose job, chin and jawline contouring, lower blepharoplasty, and the loose-skin-after-weight-loss page that names GLP-1 medications. His blog already has "Facial Changes After Weight Loss" and "Why Plastic Surgeons Keep Bashing Filler" (Oct 2026).

**Only he can say:** He is board certified in facial cosmetic surgery as well as dermatology, and he does both filler and lower blepharoplasty, so he can say when filler is the wrong answer; his own short on lower blepharoplasty versus under-eye filler does exactly that. His own line, "After more than 30 years of treating patients... less is often more", is the anti-overfilled message this theme rewards. His best videos here already prove it: an AlloClae cadaver-fat complication (61,177 views) and why he is conservative with Sculptra (43,124 views). His site already talks to the 35-to-65 patient losing weight on GLP-1s, so Ozempic face is his patients' problem, not a trend he is chasing.

**The trap:** The filler-package reel: silent before-and-afters set to music, sold as "Facial Balancing" (one clinic posted several here, all around 0.5× to 1.3× usual). Also celebrity "what did she get done" breakdowns, which look like gossip from a Park Avenue surgeon, and anything that sells a quick Ozempic-face fix like the supplement plugs in this theme.
Six to watch

`ti_7611595472540683542`: a metabolism doctor explains what Ozempic face really is; 15× usual, and he can take it one step further to the fix.

name: The derm as entertainer
short: Pimple popping, anesthesia antics, skits, lip-syncs, memes and off-topic posts.
says: Only three videos have comment data, and all three show viewers policing whether something is real or appropriate. Under a staged clip of a patient hearing he has cancer, viewers asked why it was recorded, called the doctor unprofessional and suspected it was staged. Under a PCOS weight-loss reveal, commenters argued about "normalizing taking ozempic for non-essential purposes" (a run-1 question with 1,657 likes). Under an off-topic lip-sync, viewers found it creepy until others explained the pair were siblings.

blocks.s: This is the niche's sideshow: cysts drained in close-up over pop music, patients babbling after anesthesia, dermatologists lip-syncing to trend sounds, staff skits, a meme about lip filler that "migrated", and a large share that isn't dermatology at all (celebrity edits, chiropractic cracks, anime recaps that matched the name Ariel). Most of it makes no claim; the point is a gasp or a laugh. The few that teach do it as a reaction, a dermatologist duetting someone else's clip to say the morning-shed routine is staged or the extraction tool is pushed too hard. People watch to be grossed out, to laugh, or to see a doctor be human.
The numbers

93 videos, 10% of the niche. 17% of them are winners and the median one does 0.98× its creator's usual (0.99× for the ones he could make); only 24% are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself, and nearly all of those depend on his own extraction footage or on reacting to someone else's clip.
What people claim
Most of these videos claim nothing. The ones that do:
Lip filler doesn't dissolve on its own, it migrates (a meme, 25×).
"Morning shed" routines are staged: nobody sleeps like that, and facial spray over a silicone mask does nothing (1.9×).
Extreme prosthetic-makeup clips are rage bait, and the perfect finish was probably wiped off and redone (2.0×).
Most people press too hard with a comedone extractor; counter-pressure from the other side, or two cotton swabs, causes less trauma.
Eyelid twitching is myokymia from stress, sleep loss or too much caffeine, and rest, warm compresses and time fix it.
Slathering your face in ointment before bed ("face basting") is worth your family's stares (a comedy clip, 51×).
"Skin longevity" and ageless red-carpet skin are the goal (an Oscars post with no speech, 9.7×).
There is no single "secret" behind Indian women's thick hair, and generalising about a whole group is wrong.
How it sounds

Humor is 58% of the tone. Doctors front about half of it (48%), but accounts that aren't dermatologists at all front another quarter (26%), and six of the ten biggest results belong to them. The winners rarely open with a sentence: the top video is a cyst on screen with music over it (686×), the second an anesthesiologist singing (333×), so the hook is a curiosity gap (27%), a reaction (22%) or a gross-out (12%). The one repeatable spoken pattern is the reaction stitch: "Hi, dermatologist here," then running commentary on someone else's video.
Three opening lines that worked:
“tell me your lip fillers migrated without telling me your lip fillers migrated” (@ruzannasmbatyan6739, 25×)
“Hi. Dermatologist here. Thanks to whoever tagged me.” (@dermangelo, 2.0×)
“Hi, dermatologist here to remind you that all of this morning shed content” (@dermangelo, 1.9×)
What the audience says back

Only three videos have comment data, and all three show viewers policing whether something is real or appropriate. Under a staged clip of a patient hearing he has cancer, viewers asked why it was recorded, called the doctor unprofessional and suspected it was staged. Under a PCOS weight-loss reveal, commenters argued about "normalizing taking ozempic for non-essential purposes" (a run-1 question with 1,657 likes). Under an off-topic lip-sync, viewers found it creepy until others explained the pair were siblings.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** very little, honestly; most of this theme is off-limits for him. What does map is the procedures that produce footage people stop for: excisions, mole removal, scar revision, earlobe repair, and Mohs and tumescent liposuction done under local anesthesia, where the patient is awake and can talk.

**Only he can say:** The narrow slice he can use is (1) his own procedure footage with consenting patients, framed by a surgeon who explains what you are looking at rather than just playing music over it; (2) awake-patient reactions from procedures done under local anesthesia, the honest opposite of the "funny things people say after anesthesia" compilations; and (3) a dry, deadpan reaction format, a surgeon who has taught NYU residents for years watching a bad extraction or a staged routine and saying in one line what is wrong with it.

**The trap:** A triple-board-certified surgeon in his 50s selling a "discerning clientele" on natural results gains nothing from a lip-sync, and his own two posts here (an "on this day" repost at 876 views, a Jeuveau Times Square billboard clip at 335) show it. Avoid lip-syncs, trend sounds, staff dance skits, memes, mocking patients ("You need to stop thinking that you're ugly you are"), politics and off-topic posts, and filming a patient at a vulnerable moment, which is exactly what drew "unprofessional" in the comments. Plain pimple-popping without his voice would also make the practice look like an extraction facial shop.
Six to watch
`ti_7491067437274631454`: a cyst drained in close-up over music, the theme's top result at 686×; the attention is real, and his version would add the surgeon's voice the original lacks.
`ti_7466994893387205918`: a full acne-extraction session (37×); shows that the whole procedure, not only the climax, holds an audience, if he has consenting patients to film.
`ti_7702835691071343903`: "Hi, dermatologist here" debunking a staged morning-shed routine in three sentences; the dry reaction format at its shortest (1.9×).

`ti_7702941412484009247`: a derm duets an extraction video and explains why the tool is pushed too hard and what to do instead; the low number (0.11×) aside, this is the one entertainer format a teaching surgeon owns outright.
`yo_5m58pe2-sbc`: not makeable as a meme, but at 25× "lip filler migrated" is a claim people want settled; he could answer it straight as a filler injector.

name: Lasers and the healing diary
short: CO2, Fraxel, pico, tattoo removal: what each laser does and the day-by-day recovery.
says: Very few comments were captured for this theme; the only reading is on a first-session tattoo removal clip, where viewers say it triggers trypophobia and is agony to watch. The run-1 questions fill in the rest and they are all about the week after: “does it hurt?” (254 likes), “How long is recovery?”, “How soon can you wear foundation after each session?”, “How many sessions” and “What if your skin scars super easily”. The claims point at the same worries: pain, downtime, burns on darker skin, and paying thousands for nothing.

blocks.s: This theme is the recovery, not the laser. The videos that travel are day-by-day diaries: Fraxel's brown dots darkening on day three and flaking off by day eight, a CO2 face that looks like “Freddy Krueger” but doesn't hurt, a tattoo frosting white on the first zap. Around them sit the arguments: whether laser should be the first thing you try for acne scars, whether Black skin can be lasered without burns, whether Fraxel was a waste of money, and who should be holding the handpiece. People watch to find out how bad the week after will look and whether it was worth it.
The numbers

68 videos, 7% of the niche. 22% of them are winners and the median one does 1.11× its creator's usual, rising to 1.30× for the videos Dr. Ostad could make; 56% (38 videos) are ones he could make himself. He already has 15 videos in this theme, more than in any of the other four here, and the best of them has 15,105 views.
What people claim
CO2 resurfacing tightens skin and clears pigment, pores and scars, including body scars like C-sections; “the journey may not be pretty, but the results are absolutely worth it.”
The snap of laser tattoo removal is a photoacoustic effect: light hits so hard it makes a sound wave and shatters the ink for the body to clear.
After Fraxel, the marks darken around day three (“kind of look like freckles”), mostly fade by day eight, and pores and ice-pick scars look smaller by day ten.
CO2 recovery looks frightening but isn't painful; one patient planned a month off and was healed in about a week.
Acne scars respond so well to fractional CO2 that laser should be the first thing you try, not the last.
Alexandrite lasers will very likely burn Black skin; Nd:YAG and the right operator make hair removal safe.
Non-ablative Fraxel didn't just improve appearance: years of patient data showed it cut common skin cancers by about 50%.
CO2 done too young or too hard gives a waxy look and pigment problems; it's for perioral lines in your fifties and sixties.
Before paying thousands for a laser, ask what is being treated; if the answer is the name of the machine, walk away. Fall in love with a provider, not a machine.
A CO2 laser left one patient with burn scars because the provider dismissed her pain and swelling; aftercare follow-up matters as much as the device.
Fraxel took six days to heal and gave one patient nothing visible, so “I wasted money.”
How it sounds

Confessional (31%) and reassuring (28%) lead, then clinical (21%) and salesy (19%), with a fair amount of humour (13%) around how monstrous the healing face looks. The speakers are split: doctors 29%, patients 26%, influencers 18%, brands 15%, so the patient's face is as much the star as the doctor's voice. The hook is the reveal: a before-and-after (22%), a story open (22%) or a shock shot of the treatment (12%). The winners show the ugly middle of the process within the first second.
Three opening lines that worked:
“Whoa, jump scare.” (@AvalonLaserSanDiego, 445×)
“laser tattoo removal is one of the most satisfying procedures” (@DermDocJason, 233×)
“Watch how I wasted money on a Fraxel laser treatment.” (@nainatheartist, 24×)
What the audience says back

Very few comments were captured for this theme; the only reading is on a first-session tattoo removal clip, where viewers say it triggers trypophobia and is agony to watch. The run-1 questions fill in the rest and they are all about the week after: “does it hurt?” (254 likes), “How long is recovery?”, “How soon can you wear foundation after each session?”, “How many sessions” and “What if your skin scars super easily”. The claims point at the same worries: pain, downtime, burns on darker skin, and paying thousands for nothing.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** Fraxel CO2, Fraxel Dual/Restore, Clear + Brilliant, PicoWay (including laser tattoo removal, which he offers though the makeable notes assumed he didn't), Cutera Genesis and Excel V, laser hair removal, AviClear, and pigmented lesion removal.

**Only he can say:** he did a UCLA fellowship in laser surgery as well as Mohs, so he can make the Fraxel-lowers-skin-cancer point as the surgeon who removes those cancers. He picks wavelengths by the Monk scale on his skin-of-colour page, which answers the “will it burn Black skin” fear with a method. And after 27+ years he can say which device he *won't* use on a given face, which is the “provider, not a machine” argument made from the other side of the chair.

**The trap:** what he is already posting. His 15 laser videos are device introductions (“meet my Cutera laser”) and treatment B-roll, several opening on pop-song lyrics, and none shows a patient's day three. The other trap is the gifted-influencer CO2 vlog that promises scars “gone within 1 week”.
Six to watch

`yo__PeVXKAXQ9o`: a derm explains the tattoo-laser snap over the footage (233×, 31M views); he offers PicoWay tattoo removal, so this is his to make.
`ti_7480964269807340846`: a CO2 healing diary, before to after, captioned as scary to look at but not painful (201×); the recovery format he has never filmed.

name: Salmon sperm, exosomes and copper peptides
short: PDRN, exosomes, GHK-Cu and polynucleotides: the regenerative trend, the Korean imports and the plugs.
says: Two clips came with comments, and they show both moods. Under the "exosomes replaced my routine" video, commenters object that human exosomes come from placentas without consent and warn that they are unregulated and may raise cancer risk, while a few recommend Korean exosome lines. Under a man getting salmon DNA injected in Korea, viewers are shocked and grossed out, joke about fertilizing, and some admit he is glowing. The run 1 questions point the same way: "So LED masks and collagen tablets aren't worth it?!" and "Okay but what about collagen powder?". People want to know which of these is real.

blocks.s: This theme is the Korean-import gold rush. Influencers rub on PDRN creams, film salmon sperm facials, say an exosome serum replaced their whole ten-step routine, and promise copper peptides will give the glow looksmaxxers have, usually with a discount link. The gross-out word does half the work. A small group of doctors and pharmacists push back: PDRN on bare skin does nothing, there is little evidence topical exosomes get in, the "copper uglies" are just irritation, and you should ask where your exosomes come from. People watch for the novelty and the glass-skin promise, and some for the sceptic who tells them what to throw away.
The numbers

64 videos, 7% of the niche. Only 8% of them are winners and the median one does 0.72× its creator's usual, but the makeable ones do better at 1.23×; just 31% (20 videos) are ones Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
A Korean salmon-DNA facial with microneedling leaves skin firmer and more luminous within a week (an influencer's test, 397× usual).
An exosome serum can replace your entire skincare routine.
Copper peptide (GHK-Cu) rubbed on works as well as the injected kind, and cleared one creator's acne scars.
A PDRN cream can stand in for Botox, plumping and smoothing tired skin.
If you only apply PDRN on your skin, throw it away: it needs microneedle channels to get in (a Korean pharmacist, 18× usual).
Exosomes are little packets of growth factors that tell your cells to repair, usually done as a series of three treatments.
There is no good evidence that PDRN in an eye cream penetrates enough to do anything meaningful.
Topical exosomes are among the most overhyped ingredients, with no reliable evidence they get through the skin.
The "copper uglies" aren't real: redness and peeling after copper peptides mean irritation, so stop.
Not all exosome treatments are equal: ask where they come from, because source, quality and regulation vary.
How it sounds

Influencers carry more than half of it (55%), with doctors at 17% and brands at 14%, and more than half the tone is pure sales; sponsored posts are the single biggest genre. Much of it is lip-sync or silent clips with a product in hand. The hooks that win are curiosity and disgust: "salmon sperm", a Korean secret, or a peptide every looksmaxxer supposedly uses. The sceptics who do well here open by telling you to stop or throw something away.
Three opening lines that worked:
“today I tested the treatment that are being done all in Korea” (@belleza.corea, 397×)
“Want that glowing skin all looksmaxers have?” (@TogiPeptides, 68×)
“If you just bought PDRN and only apply it on your skin, throw it away.” (@skinfo.kpharma, 18×)
What the audience says back

Two clips came with comments, and they show both moods. Under the "exosomes replaced my routine" video, commenters object that human exosomes come from placentas without consent and warn that they are unregulated and may raise cancer risk, while a few recommend Korean exosome lines. Under a man getting salmon DNA injected in Korea, viewers are shocked and grossed out, joke about fertilizing, and some admit he is glowing. The run 1 questions point the same way: "So LED masks and collagen tablets aren't worth it?!" and "Okay but what about collagen powder?". People want to know which of these is real.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** PRFM (made from the patient's own blood), exosomes (his page positions them mainly for hair), PRP hair restoration, microneedling and microinfusion, and his CEG + Ferulic serum. His blog already covers "Decoding Regenerative Aesthetics: What PRP, PRFM, PDRN, and VAMP Actually Do", "Exosomes vs PRP" and "Why Everyone Is Talking About Salmon Sperm Treatments".

**Only he can say:** He is already the press source on this: Cosmopolitan ran "Exactly What It's Like to Get Your Face Injected With Salmon Sperm" with him in September 2025. short: Hyperpigmentation and melasma, what fades them on brown and Black skin, and who treats skin of color.

blocks.s: This theme is mostly people with brown and Black skin trying to fade marks that won't leave: acne dark spots, dark underarms and elbows, and melasma that stayed after pregnancy. Influencers sell the fix (a kojic soap, a TXA serum, “results in 30 days”). Doctors mostly warn: don't do a 30% TCA peel at home, a $1,000 spa peel without prep can burn darker skin, and melasma isn't ordinary dark spots, so sunscreen and vitamin C alone won't clear it. What people claim
Never do a 30% TCA peel at home: it's a medium-to-deep peel that can burn and scar, and nobody with a medium to deep skin tone should try it.
Laser can fade acne dark spots on Black skin if the strength is kept low; that means more sessions, and it also cuts the facial hair that causes ingrown-hair spots.
Melasma is not the same as dark spots. It's driven by sun, hormones and heat, so one peel or one sunscreen won't clear it, and med-spa IPL can make it worse.
Hydroquinone is the gold standard for melasma, but you have to cycle it, two to three months on and two to three months off.
A spa's $1,000 peels without proper prep burned a client with skin of colour, and now the hyperpigmentation has to be treated.
Pigmentation in brown and Black skin gets worse with too little sunscreen, no hat, harsh acids and lasers (one derm's view; others argue the right laser is safe).
Darkness on the body that lasts longer than six weeks isn't a tan, it's pigmentation, and you can't scrub it away.
Dark underarms are mostly friction from repeated shaving.
Melasma is partly a blood-vessel problem, which is why it keeps coming back.
Skin isn't meant to be one even colour; darker elbows, knuckles and skin around the mouth are normal biology.
Only about 3% of US dermatologists are Black, which is why people struggle to find one who understands their skin.

The numbers

Ice rollers, £1,000 LED masks, collagen gummies and face-yoga gadgets aren't worth the money.

"Medical grade" isn't regulated by the FDA, so any brand can call itself that tomorrow.
Medical-grade skincare has higher concentrations of actives and improves the results of lasers and injectables.

name: Is it cancer? Spots, skin checks and Mohs
short: Moles, melanoma signs, skin checks, getting a spot removed and what Mohs surgery is.
says: The comments are personal and anxious: viewers say moles that fit the warning signs were dismissed by their own doctors, admit to health anxiety, and one who lost her mother to melanoma asks for an ABCDE video. Under the stage 4 warning-signs video, survivors and a widower share their stories, some say they had no symptoms at all, and others worry their symptoms overlap with menopause. The run-1 questions add two sharper ones: “how deadly is skin cancer?” and a viewer who asks why a basal cell that is “almost never deadly” needs Mohs at all, calling it “almost … a scam”.

blocks.s: Everyone here is asking whether a spot is going to hurt them. Doctors answer with a quiz (“Is that skin cancer or not?”), the ABCDE checklist, or a dermoscope close-up of a 2 mm melanoma nobody would spot in the mirror. Patients answer with their own bodies: stage 4 melanoma symptoms, a mole that grew under a smartwatch, an eye swollen shut the morning after Mohs. The other half is the scar. People want to see how a mole comes off, whether Mohs will wreck their face, and what it looks like at four and six weeks. They watch to be reassured, and for the case they would have missed.
The numbers

50 videos, 5% of the niche. 36% of them are winners and the median one does 5.96× its creator's usual, rising to 8.46× for the videos Dr. Ostad could make; 86% (43 videos) are ones he could make himself.
What people claim
A soft, raised mole is usually a harmless intradermal nevus; one that is asymmetric, has about three colours and is wider than 6 mm needs checking urgently.
Early skin cancer often doesn't look like a mole at all: a “pimple” that never fully heals, a dry patch no moisturiser fixes, a tiny sore that bleeds when you wash your face.
A melanoma can be 2 mm across and look normal to the naked eye; dermoscopy (“like an MRI for the skin”) is what catches it.
Change matters more than looks. The spot that grows, changes colour or looks unlike your other moles (the “ugly duckling”) is the one to worry about.
Clear Mohs slides aren't always the end: with an aggressive squamous cell cancer, an experienced surgeon keeps going and sends extra pathology to rule out spread along nerves.

Mohs takes the cancer off in thin layers and reads each one under the microscope while you wait, quoted at a 98–99% cure rate while sparing healthy skin, which is why it's the standard for the nose, ears, lips and hands.
Cosmetic moles come off three ways (laser, shave or excision), and the right one depends on the mole and where the scar will sit; an excision in the nasal crease hides the line.
A good scar after mole removal is a routine, not luck: steri-strips for at least four weeks, silicone gel or tape, and sunscreen over it every day.
A full-body skin check is quick and painless; come without makeup or nail polish, and expect the scalp, nails and tattoos to be checked.
How it sounds

Doctors carry it (52% of speakers), but patients are close to a third (32%), and the mood is clinical (44%), reassuring (38%) and confessional (38%) in roughly equal parts, with fear in a third (32%) and almost no jokes (8%). The winners open in one of two ways. Either a story starts mid-case (story open, 30%) or the viewer gets a question they must answer before the reveal (question, 20%). The plain awareness-month PSA (NHS at 0.50×, Orlando Health at 0.41×) sits near the bottom of the list, and that is the voice of his own three videos here.

“So, I recently had a really interesting Mohs case.” (@dr.truitt_sandiego, 146×)
“Signs and symptoms of stage 4 melanoma to have checked out.” (@thebecksthemess, 96×)

The comments are personal and anxious: viewers say moles that fit the warning signs were dismissed by their own doctors, admit to health anxiety, and one who lost her mother to melanoma asks for an ABCDE video. Under the stage 4 warning-signs video, survivors and a widower share their stories, some say they had no symptoms at all, and others worry their symptoms overlap with menopause. The run-1 questions add two sharper ones: “how deadly is skin cancer?” and a viewer who asks why a basal cell that is “almost never deadly” needs Mohs at all, calling it “almost … a scam”.

name: What a derm actually gets done
short: The anti-aging menu: what derms get themselves, what they'd never get, what's worth it at 30, 50, 60.
says: None of the videos in this theme came with recorded comments. The run 1 viewer questions show the demand clearly, though: "Can you make a video on retinol vs tretinoin?" blocks.s: This theme is the insider's menu. Doctors rate treatments out of ten, confess what they have had done ("I'm almost 60"), and list what they would never get, never do on their own daughter, or never spend money on. The fights are specific: threads hold a month at most, Ultherapy and EMFACE leave patients underwhelmed, Morpheus8 eats fat pads, yet another derm credits Ultherapy for ten years of lifted eyelids. Underneath runs a skincare evidence ladder: sunscreen does most of the work, retinoids are the only proven topical, glow serums have no wrinkle data. People watch because it feels like getting a straight answer from someone who knows.
The numbers
44 videos, 5% of the niche. 11% of them are winners and the median one does 0.88× its creator's usual (0.94× for the makeable ones); 77% (34 videos) are ones Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
Broad-spectrum sunscreen does 80% of anti-aging work, retinoids are the only topical proven to build collagen, and you do not need a ten-step routine.
No skincare product can smooth, tighten pores and fade spots like a retinoid, and cheap drugstore ones are fine.
Popular glow serums score close to zero on anti-aging evidence, while clinically tested peptide serums earn 10 out of 10 (a doctor's ranking, 50× usual).
A suture can't hold tissue up for longer than a month, so threads are too good to be true.
A surgeon would never get neck liposuction, under-eye Botox, filler between the eyes, a skin-only mini facelift or threads.
Ultherapy, HIFU and EMFACE leave "a complete wake of unsatisfied and underwhelmed patients"; don't use a non-surgical tool for a surgical problem.
Ultherapy lifted one derm's hooded eyes and jawline from 2014 to 2024, and works best spaced every two years.
Skip RF microneedling and PDO threads; do Sculptra, plain microneedling and Sofwave instead.
Preventative neuromodulators, including in the lower face, are the non-negotiable first step of an anti-aging plan.
An aesthetic doctor won't give her 20-year-old daughter more than 1 cc of lip filler, threads or cheek filler (7.8× usual).

“Here's 20 years of medical skincare evidence delivered in under 60 seconds.” (@drsianmew, 7.5×)
“I'm almost 60.” (@dr_ellen_marmur, 1.2×)

(1,156 likes), "Which retinoid are you using? Please recommend something budget friendly." (1,116), "Do you use retinol every day?" (600) and "Can you please do one for in your 30s?" (101). People want the doctor's own routine and a list for their own decade, not a general lecture.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** the whole menu: Botox and Jeuveau, fillers, Sculptra, Fraxel, Morpheus8, Ultherapy, thread lifts, PRFM, Clear + Brilliant, plus his Ret Nia retinoid serums, Sun Shade sunscreens and the Anti-aging Regimen Set. name: Inside the practice
short: A dermatologist's day, the job, the office, the training, and what a practice adds or announces.
says: Nothing, in this data: none of these videos has comment data recorded, and none of the 47 viewer questions from run 1 is about the practice itself. What the claims imply is that people don't know what a dermatologist does beyond Botox, are curious about the money and the hours, and, in the Ontario story, are starting to ask who is actually behind the needle at a clinic with a doctor's name on the door.

blocks.s: This is the day-in-the-life genre: dermatologists, mostly young and mostly in New York, walking the viewer through an espresso, a subway ride, a cyst excision, Botox, a Mohs case, then Pilates or a podcast. The argument underneath is that dermatologists do far more than beauty: one doctor counts 38 patients, 15 skin checks and over a hundred frozen pre-cancers in eight hours. Around it sit office tours, staff skits about the medical assistant who really runs the place, salary breakdowns and residency advice. People watch for a look behind a door they never get to open, and the videos that work show the work, not the lifestyle.
The numbers

42 videos, 5% of the niche. Only 5% of them are winners and the median one does 0.81× its creator's usual, though the ones he could make do better at 1.23×; 57% are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself. This is also where his own most-watched posts sit: five EXOMIND announcements, at 15,730 to 33,990 views each.
What people claim
A dermatologist's day can be 38 patients in eight hours, 15 full-body skin checks, over a hundred pre-cancers frozen, nine biopsies, a basal cell surgery, filler and Botox (80×).
Being triple board-certified comes from wanting to treat the whole patient, not just the skin (25×).
Dermatologists treat all hair, skin and nail disorders, and "we are not just there about the beauty."
A Mohs surgeon's morning is four Mohs cases plus an excision, each cleared under the microscope and sutured, before an afternoon of general derm and cosmetics (6.7×).
A New York derm's day runs from laser hair removal and Botox to keloid injections and a scalp cyst excision done "in record time, 10-15 minutes max" (8.1×).
The medical assistant does the intake, numbing, scheduling and training, while the doctor "just" diagnoses (a skit, 7.7×).
Ontario ending "rental" medical directors will close nurse-run clinics but make aesthetics safer, because a doctor must now meet every patient.
A cosmetic dermatologist "of course" travels the world for the best lasers, and his wife is his billboard (self-parody, 3.7×).

name: What is this on my skin?
short: Rosacea, fungal acne, milia, demodex, bumps and rashes: naming it, and what it isn't.

blocks.s: These videos give a bump, rash or patch a name, and just as often say what it isn't. Sudden forehead bumps that are yeast, not acne. Light patches that are neither a yeast infection nor vitiligo. Black dots on the nose that aren't blackheads. Pores that don't open and close. Rosacea is the biggest single topic, and the line everyone repeats is that it is controlled, never cured. Underneath runs a quieter fear: the pimple that won't heal, the "scar" that turned out to be basal cell carcinoma. People watch because a doctor names their thing in thirty seconds, and the name either calms them or sends them to book.
The numbers

40 videos, 4% of the niche. 18% of them are winners and the median one does 0.96× its creator's usual (the same 0.96× for the ones he could make), so the typical video lands at par while the top six run from 84× to 201×; 85% are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
Small red bumps that appear suddenly on the forehead and sides of the face may be yeast folliculitis, not acne (the theme's top video, 201×).
Demodex mites live in everyone's pores, come out at night to mate, can't poop, and play a role in rosacea (149×).
Light patches on the chest or back that don't respond to antifungal creams may be progressive macular hypomelanosis; "you could have the wrong diagnosis" (84×).
A facial lump dismissed as a scar and lasered turned out, at biopsy, to be basal cell carcinoma that needed Mohs (a patient's story, 183×).
A scaly red spot that "comes and goes" can be an actinic keratosis turning into basal cell, visible under the dermatoscope (20×).
A pimple that grows for weeks, bleeds, or hasn't healed in six weeks is a red flag for skin cancer.
Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disease, not "sensitive skin" or poor hygiene; alcohol is a trigger, not the cause, and it is managed, never cured.
Pores aren't doors: steam doesn't open them and cold water doesn't close them.
The tiny black dots on the nose are often trapped vellus hairs (trichostasis spinulosa), not blackheads, and scraping blackheads makes pores and pigment worse.
A rash is an emergency if it involves the eyes, mouth or genitals, blisters or sloughs, swells the face, comes with fever, or doesn't fade under a pressed glass.

blocks.s: This theme is about surviving the first months on a retinoid. The numbers

What people claim

Azelaic acid in the morning and tretinoin at night gives the benefits without the irritation, as long as you keep it off the nose and eye corners.
Most patients can't tolerate tretinoin, so a retinol or retinal used consistently is often the better choice.
0.1% and 0.05% are over-prescribed; start low, every third night, with moisturizer under and over it.

No viral influencer recipe gives everyone glass skin.

name: Acne and acne scars
short: Hormonal and adult acne, the scar types and what fills, lasers or peels each one.
says: Comments are thin here. Under the 1,274× serum video, people trade how often to apply it and purging tips, some say it made their skin worse, and skeptics say no serum beats a laser. The loudest signal is two New York women posting their own videos begging for an NYC acne dermatologist who "really cares" after Accutane and years of spironolactone stopped working. Run 1's viewer questions add the same worries: what if your skin scars easily, does this work on brown skin prone to hyperpigmentation, and what if everything except water breaks you out.

blocks.s: This theme splits in two. The first half is scars: influencers post silent before/afters crediting a serum or scar sheets, a cartoon skit promises glycolic acid and rosehip oil will "erase" pitted scars, and doctors answer with one correction: red and brown spots are marks that fade, only dents are true scars, and nothing works while you are still breaking out. The second half is stubborn adult and hormonal acne: stop washing with soap, check for PCOS, Accutane versus a vitamin A supplement. People watch because they want their old skin back and are tired of products that promised it.
The numbers
28 videos, 3% of the niche. 25% of them are winners and the median one does 1.37× its creator's usual (1.03× for the ones he could make); 61% (17 videos) are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself.
What people claim
Red or dark spots after a pimple are marks that fade on their own; only the little dents are true (atrophic) scars.
Popping pimples pushes the gunk deeper and causes the scarring.
You can't fix scars while you are still breaking out; control the acne first, then treat the dents.
There is no single best scar treatment: subcision for rolling scars, TCA cross for ice pick, RF microneedling or CO2 for texture, and 50 to 80% improvement is a realistic goal, not perfection.
Glycolic acid, vitamin C and rosehip oil used nightly will erase deep pitted scars at home.
A serum, or a pack of scar sheets, removed my acne marks and scars.
For hormonal acne, stop washing with soap: it strips the barrier and makes breakouts worse.
Adult women with acne should see a dermatologist because the cause can be PCOS.
Don't let anyone inject filler or a biostimulator into skin with active acne; it can trap bacteria.
A popular acne supplement contains about twice the adult upper limit of vitamin A, which makes supervised Accutane the safer choice.

Doctors carry slightly more than half of it (54%) and influencers about a third (36%). The tone is mostly clinical (36%) with a heavy salesy streak (25%) and real confession (21%) from people who have tried everything. The biggest view counts go to influencer before/after reveals with no useful speech, but the doctor videos that win open with the exact question the viewer is already asking, then reframe it in the next sentence ("are they actual scars or just marks?").
Three opening lines that worked:

“So the fastest way to treat hormonal acne” (@dr.victor.dermato, 17× usual)
“If you live in New York City… drop all of your dermatologist recommendations.” (@sydneycharlet, 9.2× usual)

Comments are thin here. Under the 1,274× serum video, people trade how often to apply it and purging tips, some say it made their skin worse, and skeptics say no serum beats a laser. The loudest signal is two New York women posting their own videos begging for an NYC acne dermatologist who "really cares" after Accutane and years of spironolactone stopped working. Run 1's viewer questions add the same worries: what if your skin scars easily, does this work on brown skin prone to hyperpigmentation, and what if everything except water breaks you out.

**Maps to:** AviClear ("a Proven Alternative to Accutane"), his acne page (hormonal acne in pre-menopausal women), acne scar treatments, Fraxel, Morpheus8, PicoWay, chemical peels, fillers and fat transfer for depressed scars, scar revision, and the Acne Regimen Set ($224) with the Clarifying Cleanser and Daily Pads.

**Only he can say:** he is a surgeon, so subcision, TCA cross, fat transfer and scar revision are procedures he does, not a slide he reads. His own scar page already makes the honest skin-of-colour point most people skip (lasers work better on lighter skin, microneedling suits darker skin), and the Ethnic Skin Tones page picks lasers by the Monk scale. short: Thinning hair, minoxidil, PRP for hair, scalp serums and the salon treatment called hair botox.

blocks.s: Two different conversations share this theme. One is salon "hair botox", a conditioning treatment for frizz with no toxin in it, shown off by influencers and salons in Tagalog, Portuguese and English with before-and-after flips; it gets the biggest numbers. The other is medical hair loss: dermatologists warning that minoxidil makes you shed before it works and takes months to judge, that you need a diagnosis before a treatment, that plucking grey hairs can kill the follicle, and that topical minoxidil can kill your cat. A third strand is the derm-founder story, one doctor launching her own scalp serum. People come for a verdict on what actually regrows hair.
The numbers

28 videos, 3% of the niche. 18% of them are winners and the median one does 1.32× its creator's usual, rising to 1.79× for the ones he could make; only 46% are videos Dr. Ostad could make himself, because most of the rest is salon hair botox and haircare brand launches.
What people claim
Plucking grey hairs doesn't make more grow, but plucking the same one again and again kills the follicle and leaves thin patches, so dye or trim instead (63×).
Minoxidil causes shedding in weeks 2 to 8, takes 4 to 6 months to judge, and only works while you keep using it (20×).
Constantly pulling hair back tightly causes traction alopecia, and over time that loss can become permanent (12×).

Treat the diagnosis, not the symptom: pattern hair loss needs minoxidil plus hormonal medicine, while telogen effluvium needs its trigger found.
Microneedling the scalp once a week with a stamping device, on top of daily minoxidil, boosts growth.
Topical minoxidil on hands and pillowcases can poison and kill cats, so wash hands, dry hair before bed, or ask about the oral form.

name: In the chair: PRP, microneedling and small procedures
short: PRP, microneedling, sclerotherapy, lipomas, miraDry: what the session looks like and what it's for.
says: Under a viral microneedling-with-PRP clip for acne scars, viewers ask about the risk of scarring, whether it works on brown skin prone to hyperpigmentation, what the aftercare is, what it costs and how long it lasts, and one says it went badly for them. Under Dr. Ostad's own Ellacor explainer, viewers ask whether it works on neck laxity and how many sessions it takes, and several say the short downtime is what decides it for them. The run-1 questions are the same practical list: cost, “How often would you need to keep doing this”, purging after microneedling, and microneedling versus HydraFacial.

blocks.s: This theme is about what the appointment actually looks like. Blood gets spun in a centrifuge and injected back under the eyes, a pen drags across a numbed face, veins vanish under a needle, seven lipomas come out on a lunch break. The talking is mostly practical: how many sessions, what you can't put on your skin for four days, how long the sunburn look lasts. The warnings are sharper: vampire facials at an unlicensed spa passed on HIV, and PRP is wrong for people with cancer history or blood disorders. People watch for the footage, and to decide whether they could sit through it.
The numbers

23 videos, 2% of the niche. Only 13% of them are winners and the median one does 0.74× its creator's usual (0.71× for the videos Dr. Ostad could make); 78% (18 videos) are ones he could make himself. This is a weak theme overall, carried by a couple of outliers.
What people claim
PRP is made by drawing your blood and spinning it twice, then injecting the plasma into smile lines or thinning brows.
Under-eye PRP looks wild straight afterwards, but the swelling settles within 24 hours.

What you do after microneedling matters more than the treatment: leave the serum on for at least 12 hours, no actives, retinoids or hard workouts at first, then bring them back over days four to seven.
Microneedling is a slow collagen game: you won't see an overnight change, so cap it at three or four sessions a year, and PRP only helps some people.
PRP plus microneedling once a month for four sessions, then two or three times a year, improves acne scars, pores and tone in all skin types.
The CDC linked HIV cases to vampire facials at a New Mexico spa, so PRP, Botox and filler belong only in a doctor's clinic.
PRP isn't for everyone: not with a cancer history, an active infection, active autoimmune disease or a blood or platelet disorder.
SkinPen microneedling is tolerable, with five to seven days of sunburn-like downtime that peaks on days one to three.
Lipomas can come out under local anaesthetic in a lunch break, with a week off the gym.
Ellacor removes tiny cores of skin, about 0.4 mm wide and up to 8% of the skin, to tighten the jowls without surgery (Dr. Ostad's own explainer, reposted by the brand).

Doctors speak in 43% of these, but nurses and injectors (17%), influencers (17%) and brands (13%) make up most of the rest, so it often plays like a clinic ad. The dominant hook is the procedure itself in close-up (visual shock, 22%) or a POV that puts you in the chair (17%). The two biggest winners are a wordless PRP-microneedling clip and a doctor narrating a PRP prep step by step from the first line.

“Come with me to get PRP injections under my eyes for the first time.” (@lilpeeva, 40×)
“You have micro needled your whole entire face.” (@oemcclel2, 3.0×)

name: The sunscreen fight
short: Is sunscreen toxic, does it cause cancer, is some sun good for you: the argument and the rebuttals.
says: Under the sarcastic anti-sunscreen video, viewers say they were briefly scared she meant it, some still ask whether they should wear sunscreen, and others warn that people are missing the joke. The run-1 questions show what people actually want, and it isn't the culture war: “I'm confused. Should we wear sunscreen or not?” (1,820 likes), whether a retinoid user still needs daily SPF (1,789), whether arms and other exposed skin need it every day (631), and how reapplying works over makeup (209). The confusion is practical, and nobody in this theme is answering it plainly.

blocks.s: This is an argument, not a tutorial. One side says sunscreen is toxic, chemical filters soak into your blood, some sun is good for you and the cancers it causes are generally not the deadliest ones. The other side, mostly dermatologists, answers that the sun is the number one proven cause of skin cancer, that sunscreen doesn't cause it, that vitamin D survives real-world use and that there is no safe tan. Wedged in between are sponsored launches from ISDIN, La Roche-Posay and Shiseido. People watch to see who wins, and because a melanoma survivor or a sarcastic derm makes it personal.
The numbers

21 videos, 2% of the niche. Only 14% of them are winners and the median one does 1.26× its creator's usual, falling to 0.80× for the videos Dr. Ostad could make; 67% (14 videos) are ones he could make himself, and he has made none so far.
What people claim
Some sun is good for brain and body, and the skin cancers the sun causes are mostly not the deadly kind (a podcast clip, the top performer at 66×).
Chemical sunscreen filters show up in the blood after a single application and linger for weeks, so mineral is the safer choice (2.9M views).
Sunscreen does not cause cancer: the scare comes from absorption studies and benzene-contaminated aerosol batches, and a review of 29 studies covering 313,000 people found no link.
Studies that tie sunscreen users to more skin cancer are correlation: the people who wear the most sunscreen are the ones in the sun the most.
Real-world sunscreen use has little to no effect on vitamin D levels.
There's no such thing as a safe tan; a base tan is sun damage, and everyone needs sunscreen however dark their skin.
Mineral isn't automatically better for hyperpigmentation on Black skin; broad spectrum, enough of it, and an iron-oxide tint for melasma matter more.
UV gets through clouds and windows, so wear it in winter and at your desk, and reapply every two hours to get the SPF on the label.
No study shows daily sunscreen lowers your chance of dying of skin cancer, and diligent use hasn't changed basal cell rates (a Los Angeles skin cancer surgeon, at 0.05×).
How it sounds

Contrarian is the default (67%) on both sides, with fear in 29% and open selling in 19%. Doctors are most of the speakers (57%), then influencers (24%). The dominant hook is a contrarian claim stated as fact in the first line (38%), but the videos that did best did something else: a podcast guest framing anti-sunscreen as what “most” derms quietly believe, a dermatologist playing an anti-sunscreen convert so straight that viewers thought she meant it, and a derm rating Met Gala looks by UV coverage. The earnest one-by-one myth-busts mostly land under their creators' usual.
Three opening lines that worked:
“You should probably be getting more screen time sunscreen that is.” (@dr.mamina, 32×)
“I'm a 40 year old board certified dermatologist and I seen the light” (@shereeneidriss, 20×)
“rate celebrities look from the Met Gala only from a dermatology perspective” (@drdustinportela, 1.9×)
What the audience says back

Under the sarcastic anti-sunscreen video, viewers say they were briefly scared she meant it, some still ask whether they should wear sunscreen, and others warn that people are missing the joke. The run-1 questions show what people actually want, and it isn't the culture war: “I'm confused. Should we wear sunscreen or not?” (1,820 likes), whether a retinoid user still needs daily SPF (1,789), whether arms and other exposed skin need it every day (631), and how reapplying works over makeup (209). The confusion is practical, and nobody in this theme is answering it plainly.
Ostad's angle

**Maps to:** his Sun Shade line (four zinc sunscreens, including Bronze for medium to dark skin, sold to “avoid white cast”), Lip Rescue AM SPF 30, the Hyperpigmentation Regimen Set, Mohs surgery, and his blog posts on oral sunscreen (Aug 2026) and SPF in anti-ageing.

**Only he can say:** he is a Mohs surgeon who has spent 20+ years removing the cancers this argument is about, and sits on the Skin Cancer Foundation Medical Council. He can answer “the sun's cancers aren't the deadly ones” with what a basal cell on a nose actually costs a patient, and he can answer the mineral-for-dark-skin question from a skin-of-colour page that already chooses by Monk scale.

**The trap:** a myth-bust that ends with his own $95 sunscreen. 19% of this theme is sponsored, and a skin cancer surgeon selling SPF inside a safety lecture reads exactly like those. Also, sarcasm: it won for Dr. Eidriss but confused her viewers, and he doesn't have the persona to carry it.

`in_CT7mrm4pIUt`: a derm rates Met Gala outfits purely on UV protection (1.9×); a light, repeatable format that sneaks sun protection in without a lecture.
`in_Ccz_4uJMpnj`: a derm reacts line by line to a “sunscreen is toxic” clip (1.6×); the straight rebuttal version of the fight, built for a stitch.

`yo_P686ASuuXoM` (not makeable): the “some sun is good for you” podcast clip that tops the theme (66×); this is the argument he would be answering.
